inlineContent.text: The rows reach the parser through your game’s

block, which splices everything a listed intent carries. A rule keyed on the same constant gives the verb behavior — a custom intent has no built-in default action, so any noun your rules don’t cover falls through to
(“You can’t do that.”), and costs no turn, exactly as a parse error costs none:

code: try reply("The bell tolls, deep and sonorous. Somewhere, a door unlatches.")

inlineContent.text: List several intents as one array — bare

If you forget the listing, the rule silently never fires from typed input; the bootstrap records a non-fatal warning naming the intent and the fix. It warns about the mirror mistake too — a verb you list and then wire to nothing, which the parser will match and stage 4 will have no answer for.

inlineContent.text: Every noun your rules don’t cover falls through to “You can’t do that.”, and for most verbs that is one sentence short of what the game wanted to say. Write the sentence in the
block:

code: action(.ring, reach: .directObject, say: "It is not a thing that rings.")

The rules follow from one question:
where does a noun phrase end?

A literal word and a direction slot take exactly one token each; the object and topic slots take as many as the sentence gives them. So an object slot can end wherever everything behind it has a fixed width — the phrase stops that many tokens from the end of the line — and where it doesn’t, a literal word has to close it. That, plus: a pattern starts with at least one literal word (the verb); at most one direct-object and one indirect-object slot, direct first; at most one direction slot, since a second would overwrite the first; and a topic slot ends its pattern and never mixes with a second object or a direction.

is the shape for a verb that needs both. It works because a direction slot takes exactly one token, so the split is fixed: the noun phrase is everything up to the last token. That phrase resolves like any other, so adjectives, synonyms, pronouns and disambiguation all reach it —
and
both arrive with
set.
The direction need not be the last thing in the pattern, and the noun need not stand immediately before it.
and
are two tokens of fixed width behind the noun instead of one, and split the same way.
Leave the direction off and the row asks for it:
answers
“Which way do you want to push the sandstone wall?”
, and the next line completes the command. Leave the noun off too and the bare verb asks for the noun, exactly as
does — this shape displaces nothing.
Its narrower sibling is a
literal word
beside the direction slot,
. That still works, and stays the right choice where the direction is the whole of the meaning and the noun is decoration. But the word is matched, never resolved:
stays nil, the rule cannot tell which shaft was named, and adjectives, synonyms and disambiguation all stop at the pattern. It also costs one row per spelling.
The two coexist on one intent, most specific first, which is how a game buys a fixed phrasing and a general one at once:

code: ["push", "wall", .direction],         // push wall north — no object bound
